messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

For forty-seven-year-old Minh, the world first cracked open on a Tuesday morning in the oncology ward of a county hospital. His seven-year-old daughter, Linh, had been diagnosed with a rare form of leukemia, and the smell of antiseptic—sharp, chemical, impossibly clean—had become the scent of her small body lying still under fluorescent lights. That smell, mingled with the faint, sour tang of alcohol from a hand sanitizer dispenser by her bed, now lived inside him like a splinter. He was a park ranger, a man whose days were measured in the quiet rhythm of pine needles and bird calls, but his mind had become a locked room with a single, recurring scene: the moment he first saw the IV lines, the way the dizziness had washed over him as the doctor explained the survival statistics. He had nearly fainted then, grabbing the bed rail, and that feeling of lightheadedness—a somatic echo of helplessness—had not left him since.

In the months that followed, as Linh’s treatments stabilized and she entered remission, Minh did not find relief. Instead, he found a quiet, grinding fury. He began to dwell on what other people had done to him, replaying conversations with a specialist he felt had been dismissive, with a nurse he believed had been slow to respond. He ruminated about how to get even with that specialist—drafting letters in his head, imagining a formal complaint that would strip the man of his license. This rumination, which he called "thinking things through," became a nightly ritual. He did not recognize it as a strategy, only as a necessary act of vigilance. But the more he rehearsed his grievances, the more his body responded. He would be standing in the ranger station, staring at a trail map, when the smell of antiseptic would seem to waft from nowhere—a phantom scent from the hospital that was really the memory of his own clenched jaw. Or he would feel a sudden dizziness, a spin of the room that made him grab the counter, triggered by nothing more than the sight of a white car that reminded him of the hospital shuttle. He had come to believe that these physical sensations were signs that the past was not past, that it was still happening, still threatening to pull him under.

Over the next year, Minh’s avoidance became a quiet architecture. He stopped driving past the hospital, even if it meant a forty-minute detour through the park’s back roads. He asked his wife, Kim, not to mention the specialist’s name, not to talk about the hospital at all. If a hiker on the trail mentioned a recent illness or a visit to a clinic, Minh would find an excuse to walk away—checking a fallen log, adjusting a sign—rather than endure the conversation. He had told himself this was sensible, that he was protecting his peace. But the effect was that the world shrank. He stopped attending his daughter’s school events because the gymnasium smelled faintly of bleach. He stopped visiting his own mother, who lived near the hospital, because the drive felt like a gauntlet. Kim had grown quiet, too, her patience wearing thin. She had said, just last week, "You’re not here, Minh. You’re still in that room." And he had known she was right, but he could not find a way out.

What finally brought him to the clinic was not the dizziness, nor the smell, nor the arguments with Kim. It was a single moment on the trail, three days ago, when a young boy—maybe Linh’s age—ran past him laughing, and Minh felt a surge of rage so sudden and so hot that he had to sit down on a boulder, his hands shaking. He had realized, in that moment, that he was not protecting himself; he was building a prison. He was afraid of what he might do if the rage ever broke through—afraid of the letter he might actually send, of the confrontation he might start. And so, for the first time, he had picked up the phone and called for help, not knowing if he could be fixed, but knowing he could not stay where he was.
